# AGENT.md: make this product's versus page

You are a coding agent working inside a team's product repository. They picked **versus**: a launch page that is a
race. The same task runs in two windows started at the same instant: on the left, the old way (tabs, a spreadsheet,
copy-paste, a file picker, a spinner); on the right, their product. Each lane has a clock and a click counter. The
product finishes; the old way fast-forwards to its own finish. Then a scoreboard (time, clicks, tools touched, with
where the numbers came from), the three moves that make the product quick, and the time it gives back. The same page
opened with `?record` plays all of it as one take for their launch video on X.

The page makes a claim with numbers. **Every number must be measured, by you, on real runs.** A versus page with a
flattering estimate is worse than no page: people will try it and find out. If the honest gap is small, say so, or
recommend a different format.

Read `tour/README.md` once for the engine's vocabulary. Then work through this in order.

## 0. Where things are

```
index.html            the page: the race, the score, the how strip, the ending (edit the copy here)
versus/race.js        THE NUMBERS: measured times, clicks, tools, the click log, the how strip's moments
versus/script.js      the two films: `old` (the old way) and `product`
versus/section.html   the markup as it came; versus/section.css the look, the old-way tangle and the placeholder product
versus/section.js     the race clock (don't edit unless you must)
tour/                 the engine; don't edit. tour/snapshot.py harvests real screens
kit/                  placeholder kit (press N to hide notes)
```

(In StyleFeatures: `python3 templates/scaffolds/sections/demo/tour/export.py <dest> --format versus`.)
Serve the folder with any static server, e.g. `python3 -m http.server 8000`.

## 1. Pick the task, then measure both ways for real

1. **Pick one task** a real user does often, that the product exists to make faster, and that the old way really
   does with several tools. Take it from the README, the docs' "why" section, or the launch post. Write it as the
   person doing it would say it: "Send the weekly numbers to the team", not "Streamline reporting".
2. **Write down the old way honestly.** The way a competent person does it today without the product, with the tools
   they'd really use (a spreadsheet, a dashboard, mail, a terminal). Not a strawman: no deliberately slow steps, no
   mistakes, no hunting for a button a regular user knows. If the README or issues describe the old workflow, use it.
3. **Script both workflows and time them.** For a web workflow, write a Playwright (or similar) script that does
   the old way step by step against real tools or faithful local stand-ins with realistic data, and another that
   does it in the product (its dev server with seed data). Drive them at human speed: insert realistic think and
   move times (about 0.6–1.2 s per pointer move, typing at 4–6 characters a second), and the **same** pacing for
   both. Log a timestamp for every click. Run each **five times** and take the median.
   - Or time a person: someone who knows both ways does each five times while a screen recorder runs; count clicks
     from the recording (Monet Shot shows them).
   - Waits are real: if the export takes 40 s, it takes 40 s. Don't trim either side's waits.
4. **Count**: `time` (first action to finished task, seconds), `clicks` (presses; a double-click is two; keystrokes
   don't count), `tools` (each app, site or window touched, in order). Put them in `versus/race.js`, with the click
   log of the median run in `log` if you have it.
5. **Write the `source` line** in `race.js` to say exactly how it was measured: "Median of five timed runs of each
   way by one person who uses both daily, on a 2023 laptop, with a 40-row sheet. Measured 12 March." Delete the
   placeholder text; it says these are not measurements until you do.

Never round in the product's favour, never use a best run, never compare a cold start to a warm one. If you
couldn't measure something, leave it out of the scoreboard (remove that row) rather than guess.

## 2. Put the real screens in the windows

**The product lane** (`[data-lane="new"]` in `index.html`): replace `.vs-app` with their real screens at the
window's design size (880 × 580 with the app title bar; change `data-size` and the `880/580` aspect in
`section.css` together if their app needs another shape, and keep both lanes the same size).

- **A web app: harvest it.** Run the dev server with seed data and capture each state with `tour/snapshot.py`
  (`--size 880x542` for an `app` chrome, `880x540` for `browser`), one fragment per state, hooks with
  `--hook "css=name"`. Load them with `<div data-tour-include="…">` and switch states with `show()`/`hide()` at the
  click that causes them. `tour/README.md`, *Harvested screens*, and `tour/AGENT.md`, step 2, have the details.
- **A native app: rebuild it** in static HTML/CSS from its views, with its exact tokens, icons and strings.
- Real UI copy, verbatim. Placeholders (`.ph`) where the user's own content would go. Never real customer data.

**The old-way lane**: keep it generic. Rebuild the old workflow's steps with the neutral tangle in `.vs-old`
(tabs, a dashboard, a sheet, mail, a file picker, a spinner): relabel tabs, columns and fields for their task.
**Never imitate a real company's UI** (no recognisable spreadsheet, mail or chat product, no logos or brand colours),
even if that's the tool people really use; name it in `tools` instead ("Spreadsheet", "Email").

## 3. Write the two films (`versus/script.js`)

- **`product`** is the measured run, step for step: the same clicks in the same order, at the pace of the median
  run. Its last click is the finish line unless `race.js` sets `new.time`; set it to the measured time and make the
  film's last click land there. If the film draws fewer clicks than you counted, add the missing ones.
- **`old`** is the measured old run at real speed, from the start. It plays at 1× until the product finishes, then
  the page fast-forwards the rest of the film while the clock runs on to the measured time ("Fast-forward ×n" in the
  lane). So the first stretch (as long as the product's run, plus `beat`) must be honest, real-speed footage; after
  that you may cut repetitive stretches, because the clock, not the film, carries the time. The note under the
  race says the old way's film is cut to fit; keep it.
- Every click visibly changes something. Push in (`zoom`) only on the product's result, once.
- Clocks and counters come from `race.js`, never from the films: don't try to make the films "agree" by speeding
  up the product or slowing down the old way.

## 4. The how strip and the ending

- `race.js` → `how`: the three moves that make the product quick, each a frozen moment of the product film
  (`at: '@hook'` and `after` seconds past that click). One idea each, a title with one `<em>` word, one plain line.
- The ending's big number is the old way's time minus yours, worked out from `race.js`. If the time gap is small but
  the clicks gap is large, set `lead: 'clicks'`. Fill the name, the line, the CTA and the domain in `index.html`.
- Delete every `<span class="sf-note">`, set `<title>` and the meta description.

## 5. Check it

- `index.html?t=9` freezes the race at 9 s on the wall clock. Look at the lead (`?t=0.5`), a moment in each film,
  the product finishing, the middle of the fast-forward and the end. The cursor lands on what it clicks; nothing
  outside a window; text readable.
- Play it from the top: it starts by itself a breath after it's on screen; Start both and Race again restart it.
- Phones (390 px wide) stack the lanes. Reduced motion shows the finished race, still.
- `?record&ratio=16:9`, `1:1` and `9:16` (with `&t=` to freeze): the race, the score, the how strip and the ending in
  one take. 1:1 puts each lane's clock beside its window; 9:16 stacks them.

## 6. Record and post

Open `index.html?record&ratio=16:9` (or `1:1`, `9:16`) in a large browser window and record the stage with
**Monet Shot**: crop to the stage, park the real pointer off it. It holds the first frame for 1.2 s, plays once
(about 40 s) and stops on the ending. Post the export to X with one line saying what the race is, and the link.
Keep the source line in the video: it's the reason anyone believes the numbers.


## When it's done: record your launch video with Monet Shot

[Monet Shot](https://monetshot.pages.dev/) is a free screen recorder for macOS, made for pages like this one: it frames
every take on a painting and zooms where things happen.

1. Open the finished site with `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on` (use `ratio=1:1` or `ratio=9:16` for square and vertical posts). Only the
   stage shows, it plays once from the start, and captions are on, because X autoplays muted.
2. In Monet Shot, pick the browser window, crop to the stage, and park your real pointer off it (the tour draws its
   own cursor). Record one play-through.
3. Export, and post it with a link to the site.

**For the agent:** when the site is finished, end your last message to the person with this step: the full `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on`
link on their real URL (and the 1:1 and 9:16 versions), and the Monet Shot link above.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. It is unseen between touches (a hand travelling isn't on the glass); a shadow gathers for a fifth of a second before contact, the dot flattens and darkens while pressed (`.is-down` on `.tour-cur`), and lifts away. `drag` and `swipe` carry it across the glass. Give each touch a beat: the `dur` before it is the hand travelling. Restyle the dot with `--tour-touch` / `--tour-touch-down`. `demo/phone` is the worked example. **More than one pointer.** Any pointer step with `by: 'agent'` moves a second cursor on its own track (any name works; steps without `by` move the usual one, `'main'`). Describe each in the script: ```js pointers: { main: { label: 'You', idle: 1.4 }, // a tag on the person's cursor; it fades after 1.4 s still agent: { label: 'Agent', look: 'agent', bow: .2, enter: [.33, .2] }, }, steps: [ click('@search', { by: 'agent', tag: 'search_code' }), …, click('@approve', { from: [.99, 1.03] }) ] ``` A second pointer is an arrow in `--tour-agent` (look `'agent'`) with a label tag beside it; `tag` on a step adds a word to that label from then on (the tool it's using, "waiting for you"). `bow` scales the curve of its path (0 is a straight, machine-like line), `enter` is where it first appears, `shapes: true` lets it take the hand and I-beam too. `idle: s` fades a pointer out once it has been still that long and back in when it next moves; `from: [x, y]` (fractions of the window) on a step starts that move there instead, so a hand can come back in from off the edge. Each pointer's clicks ripple in its own colour (`.tour-ring[data-who]`), and `.tour-cur[data-who="…"]` lets a page hide one (`demo/agentic` hides the person's cursor on the live page, where the visitor is the person). Touch mode (`pointer: 'touch'`) applies to the main pointer only. ### Side steps | step | what happens | options | |---|---|---| | `show(sel)` / `hide(sel)` | tweens `--in` to 1 / 0 on every match; your CSS uses `opacity: var(--in)` etc. | `dur` .35 / .28, `stagger` | | `set(sel, changes)` | instant: `{class: '+on -off'}`, `{text: 'Copied'}`, `{'--x': 2}`, `{'data-view': 'room'}`, `{attr: null}` removes | | | `tween(sel, prop, from, to)` | animates a CSS variable, `'text'` (with `fmt`) or `'scrollTop'` | `dur` .45, `fmt`, `stagger` | | `zoom(sel, z)` | camera pushes in on the target. `z` a number, or `'fit'` to frame the element at `fill` of the frame | `dur` 1.3, `fill` .66 (or `[wide, stacked]`, e.g. `[.76, .96]`: tighter on 1:1 and phones, where the window is small), `aim` | | `unzoom()` | camera back to the whole window | `dur` 1.3 | | `chapter(n, title, line)` | the card: `'02 / 05'`, a title with one `` word, one line; until the next chapter | `until` | | `caption(text)` | the caption line, until the next caption | `dur` 4 | | `mark(name)` | nothing on screen: a named moment. `tour.api.marks` lists them in order (`{ t, name }`) and `marks[name]` is that moment's time, so a page can seek to one or stop at the next (`demo/chat`'s beats, `demo/mcp`'s tabs) | | `show`, `hide` and `tween` take `ease`: `'out'` (decelerate), `'ios'` (a critically damped spring, UIKit's pushes and sheets), `'spring'` (overshoots by about 3 %), `'linear'`, or any `(t) => t` function. The default is smootherstep. The curves are exported as `eases`. `data-tour-follow` on a scrolling element (a terminal, a chat thread, a log) keeps its newest content in view every frame, so lines that `stream()` in push the old ones up. `data-tour-grow` on an element that should take height as it arrives (a message in a thread, a folded panel): the engine measures its natural height into `--h` (design px, innermost first, before targets are measured, and again on every relayout), so your CSS can open it with `--in` and let go once it's in: `max-height: max(calc(var(--in) * var(--h)), calc((var(--in) - .999) * 1e7px))`. Rows arrive smoothly and may change size afterwards. `../_chat/chat.css` is the worked example. Elements that `show()` controls should start hidden in CSS (`--in: 0`). Anything the script changes is reset when you seek backwards, because every value is recomputed from `t`. ### The camera `zoom` pushes in on a point and keeps the window filling the frame: it borrows Monet Shot's fit clamp, so a push-in never pans past the window's edge (the window is either wholly inside the frame or covers it). Zoom levels move on a log scale, so in and out feel even. Numbers are multiplied by 1.15 on portrait stages, where the window is small (not inside a `data-tour-frame`, which the window always fills). `?camera=off` turns all push-ins off. On stacked stages (1:1, 9:16, phones) the cursor fades out rather than being drawn outside the window's frame. ### Measuring Targets are measured in the window's own pixels, against the product as it is at the moment each step happens (so a button inside a modal that opens two steps earlier is measured with the modal open), and measured again whenever the layout can change: fonts loading, the stage resizing, your CSS. Edit the product freely; the script follows. ## Drivers | driver | how | when | |---|---|---| | `scroll` (default) | `data-driver="scroll"`. The section gets tall, the stage pins, scroll maps to `t`. The gate starts an auto-play drift at real speed. With `data-lock` (default on) wheel, touch and keys can't skip the film while it drifts; the Auto-play switch is the way out. A film at the very top of the page holds the page still until the first click, tap or key. | the opening of a launch page, Monet Shot style | | `play` | `data-driver="play"`. A 100svh stage with a play button, a scrubber with chapter ticks and a timecode. Space or K plays, arrows step 3 s. | a film in the middle of a page | | `manual` | `data-driver="manual"` (or `new Tour(root, script, { driver: 'manual' })`). No gate, controls or scroll handling: it draws `t = 0` and waits. The page drives it with the instance's `play()`, `pause()`, `render(t)`, `load(script)` (or `tour.api`), and may set `tour.onFrame = (t) => …`, called after every frame. `play()` dispatches `tour:end` on the root when it reaches the end. | a format with its own idea of when to play: `demo/chapters` (one film per chapter, played as you reach it), `demo/playground` | | `?t=12.5` | freezes that moment, any driver. Use it to check stills. | checking | | loop | `data-loop` on the root, `loop: true` in the script or `?loop`: the `play` driver starts again at the end, fading the window through the seam. Never in `?record`, which plays once. `begin()` (or `tour.api.begin()`) starts it from code, e.g. when it scrolls into view. | a short feature loop: `demo/launch-note` | | reduced motion | shows `still` with the camera off and the card on: the whole window, a sensible frame | always on | | `?record` | see below | recording | `data-music="audio/track.mp3"` on the root starts a loop with a fade at the gate. `data-captions`: `record` (default: only in `?record`), `always`, `off`. `data-cursor="off"` hides the cursor; `data-cursor-look="light"` gives a white arrow. ## Recording: `?record` ``` index.html?record&ratio=16:9 16:9, 1:1 or 9:16, centred in the browser window &hold=1.2 seconds held on the first frame before it plays (default 1.2) &camera=off no push-ins (see below) &captions=off no caption line &t=12.5 a frozen frame of the recording, for checking ``` It renders only the stage, at the largest box of that ratio that fits the window, on near-black, with no page, notes, spec card, gate or controls, and sizes the overlays to the stage. The film may sit anywhere in the page, inside another section: everything that isn't the film or one of its ancestors is hidden. It holds the first frame (the title band), plays once from 0 and stops on the closing frame. Captions are on, because X autoplays muted. Record it with **Monet Shot**: pick the browser window, crop to the stage, and export. Two things to know: - Monet Shot zooms on **real** clicks. The tour's clicks are drawn, not real, so Monet Shot sees none and adds no zooms of its own. The tour's camera therefore stays **on** by default. If you would rather place zooms yourself on Monet Shot's timeline, use `&camera=off` and you won't get double zooms. - Monet Shot draws its own cursor from the real pointer. Park the real pointer off the recorded window (or set Monet Shot's cursor to hidden) so only the tour's cursor shows. From script: `window.tour` has `seek(t)`, `play()`, `pause()`, `load(script)`, `t`, `duration`, `chapters` and `ready` (a promise that resolves once fonts are in and everything is measured). The root gets a `tour:end` event whenever `play()` reaches the end (any driver). **Several tours in one recorded frame.** A format whose recording is more than one film (two windows racing in `demo/versus`, a whole slide deck in `demo/deck`) makes its own element the record stage and drives the tours itself: ```js import { Tour, recordStage } from './tour.js'; const box = q.has('record') ? recordStage(root) : null; // root becomes the ratio's box, centred on near-black, the rest hidden const a = new Tour(filmA, scriptA, { driver: 'manual', record: 'page' }); // no record stage or auto-play of its own a.render(t); // the page decides t, every frame ``` `recordStage(el)` does for `el` what `?record` does for a single film (the `tour-record` and `sf-clean` classes, `--rw`/`--rh` from `&ratio=`, kept current on resize) and returns `{ w, h, ratio }`. `{ record: 'page' }` on a Tour means: in `?record` stay on the manual driver and let the page play it (captions follow `captions` as usual). Without `?record` it changes nothing. The page then holds the first frame, plays once and honours `&t=` itself. `load(script)` swaps in another script on the same window: every value the old script touched goes back to how the page drew it, then the new script is compiled and measured. `demo/playground` uses it to turn a visitor's clicks into a live script that the engine plays on from, so their clicks get the film's eases. ## Harvested screens: `include()` and `snapshot.py` ```html
``` `snapshot.py` captures an element of a running page with all its computed styles into a scoped, static fragment (`uv run tour/snapshot.py --help`). `--mobile` captures a mobile web build as a phone sees it (mobile viewport, touch, an iPhone user agent). `examples/harvest/` (in the StyleFeatures repo) is a working example: a live pricing page captured in two states and clicked through. ## Making another format Two more formats are built this way, as worked examples: `../terminal/` (a desk with a terminal and a browser, typed commands, streamed output, `ansi.py` for capturing a CLI's real output) and `../split/` (input and output panes that stack on phones). Each has its own `AGENT.md` and `export.py`. `../chapters/` (one short film per feature, stacked in a pinned slot beside the text and played on the `manual` driver as you reach it) and `../playground/` (a film, then the same product handed to the visitor: named actions in `machine.js` drive both, through `load()`) export with `export.py --format chapters|playground`. `../versus/` (two tours racing on one wall clock, the numbers from measured runs) and `../deck/` (a keynote: a tour per slide, played as the slide arrives) export with `--format versus|deck`; both use `recordStage()`. `../phone/` (a mobile app: a fingertip, iOS/Android screen transitions in `moves.js`, the phone in a `data-tour-frame`, 9:16 first) and `../launch-note/` (one shipped feature: a looping film inside a changelog post, a before/after, three notes) export with `--format phone|launch-note`. `../chat/` (the page is a conversation: the thread in the HTML is the script, played message by message, the last message the CTA) and `../mcp/` (an MCP server's page: short toured conversations, one tool each, then Add the MCP) share the chat kit in `../_chat/` and export with `--format chat|mcp`. `../agentic/` (an AI agent doing one task: a task box, then a run sheet of tool calls beside a desk of windows its own labelled cursor works, time-lapses, an approval the visitor gives, a printed receipt; three design sizes, two pointers, its own speed-controlled clock on the `manual` driver) exports with `--format agentic`. Copy `section.html`, keep the `data-tour-*` skeleton, import `tour.css` from your CSS and `Tour` from `../tour/tour.js`, and write a script. Change how it looks through `tour.css`'s tokens (`--tour-stage`, `--tour-ring`, `--tour-cap-bg`, `--tour-cap-ink`, `--tour-win-radius`) and your own `data-tour-band` / `data-tour-end`. If the engine needs a new step type, add it to `tour.js` here so every format gets it. ## When it's done: record your launch video with Monet Shot [Monet Shot](https://monetshot.pages.dev/) is a free screen recorder for macOS, made for pages like this one: it frames every take on a painting and zooms where things happen. 1. Open the finished site with `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on` (use `ratio=1:1` or `ratio=9:16` for square and vertical posts). Only the stage shows, it plays once from the start, and captions are on, because X autoplays muted. 2. In Monet Shot, pick the browser window, crop to the stage, and park your real pointer off it (the tour draws its own cursor). Record one play-through. 3. Export, and post it with a link to the site. **For the agent:** when the site is finished, end your last message to the person with this step: the full `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on` link on their real URL (and the 1:1 and 9:16 versions), and the Monet Shot link above.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. It is unseen between touches (a hand travelling isn't on the glass); a shadow gathers for a fifth of a second before contact, the dot flattens and darkens while pressed (`.is-down` on `.tour-cur`), and lifts away. `drag` and `swipe` carry it across the glass. Give each touch a beat: the `dur` before it is the hand travelling. Restyle the dot with `--tour-touch` / `--tour-touch-down`. `demo/phone` is the worked example. **More than one pointer.** Any pointer step with `by: 'agent'` moves a second cursor on its own track (any name works; steps without `by` move the usual one, `'main'`). Describe each in the script: ```js pointers: { main: { label: 'You', idle: 1.4 }, // a tag on the person's cursor; it fades after 1.4 s still agent: { label: 'Agent', look: 'agent', bow: .2, enter: [.33, .2] }, }, steps: [ click('@search', { by: 'agent', tag: 'search_code' }), …, click('@approve', { from: [.99, 1.03] }) ] ``` A second pointer is an arrow in `--tour-agent` (look `'agent'`) with a label tag beside it; `tag` on a step adds a word to that label from then on (the tool it's using, "waiting for you"). `bow` scales the curve of its path (0 is a straight, machine-like line), `enter` is where it first appears, `shapes: true` lets it take the hand and I-beam too. `idle: s` fades a pointer out once it has been still that long and back in when it next moves; `from: [x, y]` (fractions of the window) on a step starts that move there instead, so a hand can come back in from off the edge. # AGENT.md: make this product's versus page

You are a coding agent working inside a team's product repository. They picked **versus**: a launch page that is a
race. The same task runs in two windows started at the same instant: on the left, the old way (tabs, a spreadsheet,
copy-paste, a file picker, a spinner); on the right, their product. Each lane has a clock and a click counter. The
product finishes; the old way fast-forwards to its own finish. Then a scoreboard (time, clicks, tools touched, with
where the numbers came from), the three moves that make the product quick, and the time it gives back. The same page
opened with `?record` plays all of it as one take for their launch video on X.

The page makes a claim with numbers. **Every number must be measured, by you, on real runs.** A versus page with a
flattering estimate is worse than no page: people will try it and find out. If the honest gap is small, say so, or
recommend a different format.

Read `tour/README.md` once for the engine's vocabulary. Then work through this in order.

## 0. Where things are

```
index.html            the page: the race, the score, the how strip, the ending (edit the copy here)
versus/race.js        THE NUMBERS: measured times, clicks, tools, the click log, the how strip's moments
versus/script.js      the two films: `old` (the old way) and `product`
versus/section.html   the markup as it came; versus/section.css the look, the old-way tangle and the placeholder product
versus/section.js     the race clock (don't edit unless you must)
tour/                 the engine; don't edit. tour/snapshot.py harvests real screens
kit/                  placeholder kit (press N to hide notes)
```

(In StyleFeatures: `python3 templates/scaffolds/sections/demo/tour/export.py <dest> --format versus`.)
Serve the folder with any static server, e.g. `python3 -m http.server 8000`.

## 1. Pick the task, then measure both ways for real

1. **Pick one task** a real user does often, that the product exists to make faster, and that the old way really
   does with several tools. Take it from the README, the docs' "why" section, or the launch post. Write it as the
   person doing it would say it: "Send the weekly numbers to the team", not "Streamline reporting".
2. **Write down the old way honestly.** The way a competent person does it today without the product, with the tools
   they'd really use (a spreadsheet, a dashboard, mail, a terminal). Not a strawman: no deliberately slow steps, no
   mistakes, no hunting for a button a regular user knows. If the README or issues describe the old workflow, use it.
3. **Script both workflows and time them.** For a web workflow, write a Playwright (or similar) script that does
   the old way step by step against real tools or faithful local stand-ins with realistic data, and another that
   does it in the product (its dev server with seed data). Drive them at human speed: insert realistic think and
   move times (about 0.6–1.2 s per pointer move, typing at 4–6 characters a second), and the **same** pacing for
   both. Log a timestamp for every click. Run each **five times** and take the median.
   - Or time a person: someone who knows both ways does each five times while a screen recorder runs; count clicks
     from the recording (Monet Shot shows them).
   - Waits are real: if the export takes 40 s, it takes 40 s. Don't trim either side's waits.
4. **Count**: `time` (first action to finished task, seconds), `clicks` (presses; a double-click is two; keystrokes
   don't count), `tools` (each app, site or window touched, in order). Put them in `versus/race.js`, with the click
   log of the median run in `log` if you have it.
5. **Write the `source` line** in `race.js` to say exactly how it was measured: "Median of five timed runs of each
   way by one person who uses both daily, on a 2023 laptop, with a 40-row sheet. Measured 12 March." Delete the
   placeholder text; it says these are not measurements until you do.

Never round in the product's favour, never use a best run, never compare a cold start to a warm one. If you
couldn't measure something, leave it out of the scoreboard (remove that row) rather than guess.

## 2. Put the real screens in the windows

**The product lane** (`[data-lane="new"]` in `index.html`): replace `.vs-app` with their real screens at the
window's design size (880 × 580 with the app title bar; change `data-size` and the `880/580` aspect in
`section.css` together if their app needs another shape, and keep both lanes the same size).

- **A web app: harvest it.** Run the dev server with seed data and capture each state with `tour/snapshot.py`
  (`--size 880x542` for an `app` chrome, `880x540` for `browser`), one fragment per state, hooks with
  `--hook "css=name"`. Load them with `<div data-tour-include="…">` and switch states with `show()`/`hide()` at the
  click that causes them. `tour/README.md`, *Harvested screens*, and `tour/AGENT.md`, step 2, have the details.
- **A native app: rebuild it** in static HTML/CSS from its views, with its exact tokens, icons and strings.
- Real UI copy, verbatim. Placeholders (`.ph`) where the user's own content would go. Never real customer data.

**The old-way lane**: keep it generic. Rebuild the old workflow's steps with the neutral tangle in `.vs-old`
(tabs, a dashboard, a sheet, mail, a file picker, a spinner): relabel tabs, columns and fields for their task.
**Never imitate a real company's UI** (no recognisable spreadsheet, mail or chat product, no logos or brand colours),
even if that's the tool people really use; name it in `tools` instead ("Spreadsheet", "Email").

## 3. Write the two films (`versus/script.js`)

- **`product`** is the measured run, step for step: the same clicks in the same order, at the pace of the median
  run. Its last click is the finish line unless `race.js` sets `new.time`; set it to the measured time and make the
  film's last click land there. If the film draws fewer clicks than you counted, add the missing ones.
- **`old`** is the measured old run at real speed, from the start. It plays at 1× until the product finishes, then
  the page fast-forwards the rest of the film while the clock runs on to the measured time ("Fast-forward ×n" in the
  lane). So the first stretch (as long as the product's run, plus `beat`) must be honest, real-speed footage; after
  that you may cut repetitive stretches, because the clock, not the film, carries the time. The note under the
  race says the old way's film is cut to fit; keep it.
- Every click visibly changes something. Push in (`zoom`) only on the product's result, once.
- Clocks and counters come from `race.js`, never from the films: don't try to make the films "agree" by speeding
  up the product or slowing down the old way.

## 4. The how strip and the ending

- `race.js` → `how`: the three moves that make the product quick, each a frozen moment of the product film
  (`at: '@hook'` and `after` seconds past that click). One idea each, a title with one `<em>` word, one plain line.
- The ending's big number is the old way's time minus yours, worked out from `race.js`. If the time gap is small but
  the clicks gap is large, set `lead: 'clicks'`. Fill the name, the line, the CTA and the domain in `index.html`.
- Delete every `<span class="sf-note">`, set `<title>` and the meta description.

## 5. Check it

- `index.html?t=9` freezes the race at 9 s on the wall clock. Look at the lead (`?t=0.5`), a moment in each film,
  the product finishing, the middle of the fast-forward and the end. The cursor lands on what it clicks; nothing
  outside a window; text readable.
- Play it from the top: it starts by itself a breath after it's on screen; Start both and Race again restart it.
- Phones (390 px wide) stack the lanes. Reduced motion shows the finished race, still.
- `?record&ratio=16:9`, `1:1` and `9:16` (with `&t=` to freeze): the race, the score, the how strip and the ending in
  one take. 1:1 puts each lane's clock beside its window; 9:16 stacks them.

## 6. Record and post

Open `index.html?record&ratio=16:9` (or `1:1`, `9:16`) in a large browser window and record the stage with
**Monet Shot**: crop to the stage, park the real pointer off it. It holds the first frame for 1.2 s, plays once
(about 40 s) and stops on the ending. Post the export to X with one line saying what the race is, and the link.
Keep the source line in the video: it's the reason anyone believes the numbers.
